opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think of deep learning as mostly an experimental science right now, maybe more like alchemy or early chemistry than physics. We have some intuitions and some math, but they usually come after the fact. You try something, it works or it doesn't, and then you tell yourself a story about why.

I even joked about this in a paper once. We tried a bunch of gated activation variants in the transformer feed-forward layer, some of them worked noticeably better, and I wrote that we offer no explanation and attribute the success to divine benevolence. That was half a joke, but only half. A lot of the time you really don't know why something works, and pretending you do can mislead people.

So I think the right attitude is to be very empirical and very humble. Run lots of experiments, make them cheap and fast so you can try many ideas, and believe the results even when they contradict your intuition. The explanations matter, because a good mental model helps you guess what to try next, but I treat them as hypotheses. If the theory says something shouldn't work and the experiment says it does, the experiment wins.

The other thing is scale. Many tricks look great on small models and vanish at scale, and some things only start to matter once you go big. So part of experimenting well is figuring out what you can learn cheaply at small scale that still predicts what happens on the big runs. That's where a lot of the real skill is, and where I think the intuition gets built, not from theory first, but from having run a thousand experiments and seeing the patterns.

r001.rationale: The response compares deep learning to “alchemy or early chemistry” and says researchers often do not know why methods work.

r002.rationale: It treats explanations as hypotheses and says experiments decide whether they hold up, including when results contradict the theory.

fable-5.1.text:
I think experimentation is basically the whole game right now, because honestly, we don't understand why most of this stuff works. We have intuitions, we have stories we tell afterwards, but the theory is way behind the practice. So you try something, you look at the loss curve, and the loss curve is the truth. It doesn't care about your elegant explanation.

A lot of the things that ended up mattering, like attention or mixture of experts, came out of having some hunch, running the experiment, and then being surprised. And the surprise is where the understanding comes from. If you only ran experiments that confirmed what you already believed, you'd learn nothing. The failures are almost more informative, because they tell you your mental model was wrong somewhere.

The thing I'd emphasize is iteration speed. The faster you can go from idea to result, the more ideas you can test, and the more of those surprising results you get to see. So a big part of doing good research is just engineering the loop to be tight: small models, quick turnaround, clean comparisons. If an experiment takes a month, you'll only run a handful and you'll overfit to your prior. If it takes an hour, you can be genuinely curious.

And then you have to be careful about what you're actually learning. A lot of findings don't survive scale. Something helps at a small size and vanishes at a large one, or the reverse. So part of the discipline is testing across a range of scales and being humble about extrapolating. But I'd still take an empirical result over a beautiful argument almost every time. The field has been humbled too many times by things that shouldn't work and do.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers understand little about why AI methods work and that theory lags practice, but it does not compare the field to alchemy.

r002.rationale: The response describes testing hunches and learning from surprising results, but does not clearly state that explanations for why a method works typically need further experiments to establish whether they are correct.

astra-6.text:
I think experimentation is essential. You have some intuition about why a method ought to work, but there are usually a lot of plausible explanations, and the experiment helps you distinguish between them. Change one thing, see what happens, and then try to predict what will happen in the next experiment.

There’s also a difference between finding something that works and understanding why it works. You can get a useful result before you have a satisfying explanation. That’s fine—as long as you don’t confuse your explanation with evidence. Ideally, the explanation lets you make better predictions and find the next improvement.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare contemporary AI research to alchemy or describe it as having limited understanding of why methods work.

r002.rationale: It says there are usually multiple plausible explanations and experiments help distinguish among them, then emphasizes not confusing explanations with evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think experimentation is how you find out which of your intuitions are actually useful. You have some story about why a method should work, but usually there are a lot of things changing at once, so the result doesn’t tell you whether that story is right.

You want to make a prediction, change something, and see what happens. And often the most informative result is the one that surprises you. If you remove something you thought was essential and the model gets better, that’s a good opportunity to update your understanding.

There’s also a distinction between finding something that works and understanding why it works. You can make progress on the first without having a complete answer to the second. I wouldn’t want to stop useful experiments while waiting for a beautiful explanation. Ideally, the experiments and the explanations keep pushing each other forward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limited understanding of why methods work but does not compare contemporary AI research to alchemy.

r002.rationale: It says a proposed explanation may not be established by results when many things change, and recommends making a prediction, changing something, and observing the result to test it.
